items.p: Which business structure is owned, controlled and run by one person?
items.a: Sole trader
items.ref: Sole traders are small businesses owned, controlled and run by one person.

items.p: What does 'unlimited liability' mean for a sole trader?
items.a: They are personally responsible for all the debts of the business
w: The debts belong only to the bank
The business has no legal obligations
items.ref: Sole traders have unlimited liability: they are personally responsible for all debts incurred in their business.

items.p: What is a 'sleeping' partner in a limited partnership?
items.a: A partner who only provides capital
w: A partner who runs the business every day
A partner who is also an employee
items.ref: In limited partnerships, 'sleeping' partners only provide capital.

items.p: How are profits divided between the shareholders of a limited company?
items.a: According to the number of shares they hold
items.ref: Profits are divided between the shareholders based on the number of shares they hold (dividends).

items.p: How is decision-making usually managed in a cooperative?
items.a: Democratically: each member has one vote
w: The founder with most money decides
Votes depend on the shares owned
items.ref: Cooperatives are usually run in a democratic way: each member has one vote in decision-making.

items.p: Who is the franchisor?
items.a: The company that sells the right to use its business idea
w: The person who buys the right to copy the business
The bank that finances the business
items.ref: The franchisor sells the right to use a business idea in a new location.

items.p: What does a franchisee pay to the franchisor?
items.a: An initial fee and a percentage of the annual turnover
w: Only the taxes of the franchisor
items.ref: The franchisee pays an initial sum (franchise fee) and a percentage on the annual turnover (management service fee).

items.p: Why is franchising a low-risk way of starting a business?
items.a: It uses an already tested and successful business model
w: Because it needs no money at all
Because the franchisee can change the model freely
Because the government pays the costs
items.ref: Franchising uses an already tested and successful business model, which lowers the possibility of failure.

items.p: Which is a disadvantage of franchising?
items.a: Limited flexibility and innovation
w: Difficulty in raising finance from banks
items.ref: The business model cannot be changed by the franchisee, so flexibility and innovation are limited.

items.p: What is typical of a start-up?
items.a: High costs and limited financial resources at the beginning
w: A very old and traditional structure
Guaranteed success in the first year
items.ref: Start-ups begin with high costs and limited financial resources, so they look for capital from several sources.

items.p: What is internal growth?
items.a: A company uses its own resources to expand
w: A company merges with another one
A company is bought by a larger one
items.ref: In internal growth a company uses its own resources (new assets, new lines of product). It is more gradual.

items.p: What is vertical integration?
items.a: Businesses at different stages of production join together
w: Businesses at the same stage join together
A company opens a new shop
items.ref: Vertical integration: businesses operating at different stages of production join together.

items.p: What is a takeover (or acquisition)?
items.a: A business buys another one, entirely or some of its shares
w: Two similar companies form a new one
items.ref: In an acquisition or takeover a business buys another one, either entirely or some shares.

items.p: When does a parent company control a subsidiary?
items.a: When it owns or controls more than 50% of the voting shares
w: When it owns 10% of the shares
When it has the same name
When it is in the same country
items.ref: A parent company either owns or controls more than 50% of the voting share in the subsidiary.

items.p: Why are multinationals often the reason for debates?
items.a: Dominance of the market, cheap labour exploitation and tax avoidance
items.ref: Debates are about market dominance, exploitation of cheap labour in developing countries and tax avoidance.

Q4.title: Quiz 4 · Internal organisation of a company

items.p: Why does a growing company need an internal organisation?
items.a: So that everybody understands their role and how to cooperate
w: To reduce the number of products
items.ref: A company needs an internal organisation so that everybody knows their role and how to cooperate.

items.p: What does an organigram show?
items.a: The structure of the departments and the chain of command
items.ref: Organigrams graphically represent the structure of the departments and show the chain of command.

items.p: Who is at the top of an organigram?
items.a: The Board of Directors and the CEO
items.ref: On the top of an organigram you find the Board of Directors and the CEO.

items.p: What is outsourcing?
items.a: Contracting work out to external organisations
w: Moving production back to the home country
items.ref: Outsourcing involves contracting work out to external organisations.

items.p: What is reshoring?
items.a: A business returns production to the country of origin
w: A business opens a branch abroad
items.ref: Reshoring is when a business returns production or operations to the country of origin; it is the reverse of offshoring.

items.p: What is CSR?
items.a: The attempt of companies to generate a positive social impact
w: A tax paid to the government
items.ref: CSR is the attempt of companies to manage their business processes so as to generate a positive social impact.

items.p: Which of these are stakeholders?
items.a: Customers, suppliers, employees, shareholders and communities
items.ref: Stakeholders include customers, suppliers, employees, shareholders, communities and the environment.

items.p: What does 'win-win' mean for CSR?
items.a: Both society and the company benefit
items.ref: CSR is a win-win strategy: it benefits society and the business as well.

items.p: Which type of CSR is about donating money to worthy causes at local level?
items.a: Philanthropic responsibility
items.ref: Philanthropic responsibility: improving society, for example donating money to worthy causes.

items.p: Which is an advantage of a CSR strategy?
items.a: Increase in customers' retention and loyalty
items.ref: CSR improves public image, finances, customer loyalty and employees' engagement.
